subject: physics
topicDisplay: Theme E · Nuclear Physics (Atom, Decay, Fission, Fusion & Stars)
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: The nucleus of an atom contains:
questions.explain: Protons and neutrons (nucleons) form the dense, positively charged nucleus; electrons orbit it.

questions.q: Isotopes of an element have the same number of protons but different numbers of:
questions.explain: Isotopes share atomic number but differ in neutron number and hence mass number.

questions.q: The force that holds protons and neutrons together in the nucleus is the:
questions.explain: The strong nuclear force acts over very short ranges to overcome proton-proton repulsion.

questions.q: Radioactive decay is described as random and spontaneous, meaning it:
options: Cannot be predicted for an individual nucleus and is unaffected by external conditions
questions.explain: Decay is a random process for each nucleus, unaffected by temperature, pressure or chemical state.

questions.q: An alpha particle is:
questions.explain: Alpha radiation is a helium-4 nucleus; it is highly ionising but weakly penetrating.

questions.q: A beta-minus particle is:
questions.explain: Beta-minus decay emits an electron (and an antineutrino) when a neutron becomes a proton.

questions.q: Gamma radiation is:
questions.explain: Gamma rays are highly penetrating electromagnetic radiation, carrying no charge or mass.

questions.q: Which type of radiation is stopped by a sheet of paper?
questions.explain: Alpha is the least penetrating; beta is stopped by aluminium and gamma by thick lead/concrete.

questions.q: The half-life of a radioactive isotope is the time for:
options: Half the nuclei in a sample to decay
questions.explain: After each half-life the number of undecayed nuclei (and the activity) halves.

questions.q: A sample has a half-life of 5 days. After 15 days, the fraction remaining is:
questions.explain: 15 days = 3 half-lives; remaining fraction = (1/2)^3 = 1/8.

questions.q: After 2 half-lives, the activity of a radioactive source is what fraction of its original value?
questions.explain: Each half-life halves the activity: (1/2)^2 = 1/4.

questions.q: In nuclear notation, the top number (e.g. 14 in carbon-14) is the:
questions.explain: The mass number A = protons + neutrons; the bottom number is the atomic (proton) number Z.

questions.q: Nuclear fission is the process in which a large nucleus:
options: Splits into smaller nuclei, releasing energy
questions.explain: Fission of heavy nuclei (e.g. uranium-235) releases energy and neutrons.

questions.q: A chain reaction in a fission reactor is sustained because each fission:
options: Releases neutrons that can cause further fissions
questions.explain: Emitted neutrons trigger more fissions; control rods absorb excess neutrons to control the rate.

questions.q: The energy released in nuclear reactions comes from a small loss of mass, related by:
questions.explain: A mass defect is converted to energy according to Einstein's mass-energy equivalence.

questions.q: In a nuclear reactor, control rods are used to:
options: Absorb neutrons and control the reaction rate
questions.explain: Inserting control rods absorbs neutrons, slowing or stopping the chain reaction.

questions.q: Nuclear fusion is the process in which:
options: Light nuclei join to form a heavier nucleus, releasing energy
questions.explain: Fusion of light nuclei (e.g. hydrogen to helium) powers stars and releases large amounts of energy.

questions.q: The energy source of stars like the Sun is:
options: Nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium
questions.explain: Fusion in the core converts hydrogen to helium, releasing the energy that makes stars shine.

questions.q: Fusion requires extremely high temperatures and pressures because:
options: Nuclei must overcome their electrostatic repulsion to get close enough
questions.explain: Only at very high energies can positively charged nuclei approach closely enough for the strong force to bind them.

questions.q: Elements heavier than helium are largely produced in stars by:
questions.explain: Successive fusion in stars, and explosive supernovae, build up heavier elements.
